title: Masquerading: Masquerade Task or Service
summary: Masquerading a task or service means giving a persistence object a name, display name or description that copies or closely resembles a legitimate one, so that a reviewer scanning a list of scheduled tasks or services sees nothing that stands out. The technique only changes labels and descriptive text; the executable that the object actually launches is what performs the malicious work, which is why name-based review is a weak control. Scheduled tasks on Windows and systemd unit files on Linux both carry human-readable fields that operators trust at a glance, and a single character change, an extra space or a plausible description is often enough to pass casual inspection. Defenders identify the behaviour by reviewing the action, trigger and account of every new or modified task and service against a known baseline, and by watching the configuration database, the task scheduler operational log or unit file changes on disk. Legitimate software installs and updates also create tasks, so the discriminator is the image and command line being launched rather than the label attached to it.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker creates a scheduled task or a system service and gives it a name that sounds normal. A task is a job the computer runs on a schedule. A service is a program that runs in the background. The label looks harmless, so nobody checks it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Administrators review long lists of tasks and services by reading names. A familiar name is usually ignored. Attackers use that habit to keep their program running after a reboot. The name says backup or update, but the program is not. Only the details behind the name reveal the truth.
howItWorks: The attacker creates a scheduled task or a background service on the machine.
They set the task or service to start at a fixed time or at every boot.
They choose a name that copies a known good task or one that simply sounds official.
They also fill the description field with dull, believable wording.
The object points at the attacker program, which runs with the chosen account.
Anyone reading only the name sees something that belongs on the system.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where the door keys hang on labelled hooks. A stranger adds a new key on a hook labelled spare front door. It looks like it belongs there. Nobody asks who put it up, because the label is familiar.
takeaways: Read what a task or service runs, not just what it is called.
Compare new tasks and services against a known good baseline.
A believable description field is cheap to write and proves nothing.

objectives: Explain how labels and descriptions on tasks and services can be made to look legitimate.
Identify the fields that reveal what a task or service actually executes.
Describe which logs and configuration stores record task and service changes.
Separate this sub-technique from the parent masquerading technique.
Explain why baseline comparison beats name review for detection.
